title: The Silver Cup and Judah’s Plea
summary: Joseph hides his silver cup in Benjamin’s sack to test his brothers; Judah confesses their guilt before God and offers himself as a slave in Benjamin’s place.
historicalContext: The scene falls in the second year of the famine (45:6), about twenty-two years after the brothers sold Joseph, when he was nearly forty and governed Egypt’s grain under Pharaoh. Great Egyptian households were run by a chief steward who handled provisions, guests, and business, which is the role of the man “over his house” here. Bowls and goblets were used across the ancient Near East to read omens from the patterns of oil, water, or wine poured into them, and such a vessel belonging to a high official would be counted precious and in some sense sacred. Stealing property from a temple or palace drew the death penalty in Mesopotamian law, so the brothers’ offer in verse 9 is extreme yet not unthinkable. Egyptian tomb reliefs show Asiatic petitioners lying face down before high officials, and the language of suretyship, in which one person pledges himself for another, belongs to the commercial and family law of the period.
literaryContext: Genesis 44 brings the brothers’ second journey to Egypt to its crisis and sets up Joseph’s self-disclosure in chapter 45. It mirrors chapter 43, with a commission to the steward, a nervous exchange with him, and an audience before Joseph, but its deeper echo is chapter 37. Joseph re-creates the old situation: Rachel’s remaining son stands apart, apparently guilty, and the ten are free to go home without him. Key words carry the theme. “Evil” is charged against the brothers (vv. 4-5) and returns in Judah’s dread of the evil that would come on his father (v. 34); the verb “find” runs through the search and peaks in Judah’s confession that God has found out their iniquity (v. 16); and the word for “instead of” links evil repaid for good (v. 4) with Judah’s offer to stay in Benjamin’s place (v. 33). Judah’s plea, the longest speech in Genesis, mentions their father again and again and shows how far the man who proposed selling Joseph (37:26-27) has come.
themes: A test that exposes the heart
Conscience and confession of past sin
Substitution: one offered in another’s place
Love for a father and a favoured brother

outline.title: The Cup in Benjamin’s Sack
outline.summary: Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack, sends his steward after the departing brothers with a charge of theft, and the cup is found; the brothers tear their clothes and all return to the city.

outline.title: Confession before Joseph
outline.summary: The brothers fall before Joseph, Judah confesses that God has found out their iniquity and offers all of them as slaves, and Joseph insists that only Benjamin will stay.

outline.title: Judah Recounts the Family’s Story
outline.summary: Judah approaches the ruler and retells their dealings with him and with their father, stressing Jacob’s love for Benjamin and his grief for the son he believes was torn in pieces.

outline.title: Judah Offers Himself in Benjamin’s Place
outline.summary: Judah explains that losing Benjamin would kill his father, recalls his pledge as surety for the lad, and begs to remain as a slave instead of him.

verses.bibleText: And he commanded the steward of his house, saying, Fill the men's sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put every man's money in his sack's mouth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The banquet of 43:31-34 is over, and the brothers expect to leave in the morning with grain, with Simeon restored, and with Benjamin safe. Overnight Joseph sets his final test in motion. He gives orders to “the steward of his house,” the same trusted official who brought the brothers into Joseph’s home and calmed their fears about the returned money (43:16-24). That steward is clearly party to the plan from start to finish, which matters when his words are weighed in verse 5.

Two instructions come first. The sacks are to be filled “as much as they can carry,” a generous detail that goes beyond the first journey (42:25). And each man’s money is to be put back in his sack’s mouth once more. The narrator never mentions this money again; the cup will overshadow it. Yet it has a purpose. The brothers had already been unnerved by money that appeared without explanation, and the steward had told them that their God had given them treasure in their sacks (43:23). A second return can only deepen their sense that an unseen hand is dealing with them.

Joseph is not playing a cruel game. He needs to know whether the men who sold him have changed, and words alone cannot tell him. As God once “did tempt Abraham” to bring out what was in his heart (22:1), Joseph arranges a situation that will show what is in theirs. Testing in Scripture often serves this purpose of revealing character (Deuteronomy 8:2), and the end in view here is reconciliation.

The narrator lets the reader see the preparations before the brothers feel their effect. That arrangement places us beside Joseph, knowing more than the travellers do, and it keeps attention on the question the chapter is written to answer: what will these men do when the choice of chapter 37 is set before them again?

wordNotes.term: אֲשֶׁר עַל־בֵּיתוֹ (’asher ‘al-beyto) — the steward of his house
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the one who is over his house.” The phrase names the chief manager of a great household, responsible for its property, servants, and guests. Joseph himself had held this kind of post in Potiphar’s house (39:4), and Pharaoh had set him “over my house” in a far larger sense (41:40). Later the same title is used for high palace officials in Israel (1 Kings 4:6; Isaiah 22:15).

verses.bibleText: And put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack's mouth of the youngest, and his corn money. And he did according to the word that Joseph had spoken.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The Hebrew word order throws the cup to the front of the sentence: “and my cup, the silver cup, put in the sack’s mouth of the youngest.” Everything else in Joseph’s instructions serves this. The vessel is a goblet or bowl, larger and finer than an everyday drinking cup, and the repeated description, “my cup, the silver cup,” marks it as valuable and personal. It may well have been on the table at the feast the night before, where Benjamin sat as the guest of honour (43:34).

The choice of Benjamin is the heart of the plan. Twenty-two years earlier the brothers had resented the favoured son of Rachel and sold him. Now Rachel’s other son has just been openly favoured by the lord of Egypt, served five times as much as the rest. If the cup turns up in his sack, he will look guilty and the others innocent. Joseph has built a situation in which the ten can abandon Benjamin with a clear conscience and an excuse their father could hardly dispute. Whether they do so will show what kind of men they have become.

There is also a sharp irony in the metal. The brothers once took silver for Joseph, twenty pieces from the Ishmaelites (37:28). Now a silver cup will make them look like thieves, and their own silver, returned in every sack, will lie beside it. The phrase “his corn money” ties Benjamin to the same treatment as the others, so that the only difference between his sack and theirs is the cup.

The verse closes with the steward’s exact obedience: “he did according to the word that Joseph had spoken.” Joseph controls every step. The reader knows what the brothers do not, and that gap between knowledge and ignorance drives the suspense of the whole chapter.

wordNotes.term: גְּבִיעִי גְּבִיעַ הַכֶּסֶף (gevi‘i gevia‘ hakkesef) — my cup, the silver cup
wordNotes.explanation: Gevia‘ is a goblet or bowl, distinct from the ordinary kos, “cup” (40:11). It names the bowls of wine set before the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:5) and the almond-shaped cups on the branches of the tabernacle lampstand (Exodus 25:33). The word therefore suggests an ornamented vessel of some size and value, fit for a great man’s table.

verses.bibleText: As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away, they and their asses.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“As soon as the morning was light,” the brothers set out. Everything seems to have gone right. They had feared arrest on arrival and instead were feasted; Simeon was restored to them; Benjamin, whose safety Judah had guaranteed, was with them; and their donkeys were loaded with grain. They had even “drunk, and were merry” with the governor (43:34). The early start shows men eager to be home with good news for an anxious father.

The short, plain sentence lets the reader feel the calm before the blow. “The men” and “their asses” move off together, and nothing suggests that they have looked into their sacks. Morning departures mark several turning points in Genesis (19:27; 22:3; 28:18), and this one, which begins in relief, will end the same day with the brothers back in Joseph’s house on their faces.

The reader, unlike the brothers, knows what is packed in the sacks. That knowledge turns an ordinary departure into a scene of suspense. Each mile they put behind them feels like safety to the travellers, while the reader waits for the steward to appear on the road.

wordNotes.term: הַבֹּקֶר אוֹר (habboqer ’or) — the morning was light
wordNotes.explanation: A compact clause, literally “the morning was light,” marking first daylight. The verb ’or, “to become light,” is the root of the light called forth on the first day (1:3), and Achish uses it when he sends David away “as soon as ye have light” (1 Samuel 29:10). Here it fixes the hour of departure and hints at how quickly the day will turn.

verses.bibleText: And when they were gone out of the city, and not yet far off, Joseph said unto his steward, Up, follow after the men; and when thou dost overtake them, say unto them, Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph waits until the brothers have left the city but are “not yet far off.” The timing is deliberate. They are far enough away to look like fugitives and near enough to be brought back quickly to his house. The city is not named, though it was evidently the seat of Joseph’s administration.

The steward is given his words in advance: “Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?” The charge is ingratitude as much as theft. The brothers had been welcomed, fed, and honoured at the governor’s table; to steal from such a host would violate the sacred obligations of hospitality that ran deep in the ancient world. David later voiced the same complaint against Nabal, “he hath requited me evil for good” (1 Samuel 25:21), and the psalmist laments enemies who “rewarded me evil for good” (Psalm 35:12). Proverbs warns that evil will not leave the house of the one who does this (Proverbs 17:13).

The question cuts deeper than the brothers can yet know. Years before, Joseph had come to them in Dothan on an errand of kindness, sent by their father to ask after their welfare (37:14), and they repaid him by stripping him and selling him. They are innocent of the cup, but the accusation describes exactly what they once did.

The same pairing of evil and good will return at the end of Genesis, transformed. Joseph will tell his brothers, “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (50:20). Human beings may return evil for good; God can turn evil into good.

wordNotes.term: שִׁלַּמְתֶּם רָעָה תַּחַת טוֹבָה (shillamtem ra‘ah tachat tovah) — rewarded evil for good
wordNotes.explanation: Shillem means to repay or make good, from the same root as shalom, wholeness. Here it is used ironically: instead of returning good, the men are accused of paying back evil. The preposition tachat, “in place of,” reappears in verse 33, where Judah asks to remain “instead of the lad.” The chapter moves from evil exchanged for good to one man offered in exchange for another.

verses.bibleText: Is not this it in which my lord drinketh, and whereby indeed he divineth? ye have done evil in so doing.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The steward is to add, “Is not this it in which my lord drinketh, and whereby indeed he divineth?” He speaks as though the brothers know exactly what is missing, which heightens the sense that their guilt is already plain. The cup is not only valuable; it is presented as the instrument by which the great man discerns hidden things. To steal it would be theft, ingratitude, and sacrilege at once: “ye have done evil in so doing.”

The practice in view was common in the ancient Near East. A diviner would pour water, oil, or wine into a bowl, sometimes with small objects dropped in, and read the shapes and movements on the surface as messages about the future, the source of a trouble, or a person’s guilt. Egyptians of rank were expected to have access to such arts, and Joseph’s reputation for insight could easily be attributed to them by those around him.

The narrative itself makes clear that Joseph is playing a part. He did not need a cup to know who had “taken” it; he had ordered it placed in Benjamin’s sack. The steward who speaks the line is his accomplice and repeats words he was given (v. 6). The claim belongs to Joseph’s disguise as an Egyptian official, the same disguise that included speaking through an interpreter (42:23) and seating the brothers by age to unsettle them (43:33). It is meant to make the brothers feel that nothing can be hidden from this man and to drive them past pretence.

Scripture leaves no doubt about divination itself. Israel was told, “neither shall ye use enchantment” (Leviticus 19:26), and Moses later listed the diviner among those whose practices are an abomination to the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Balaam confessed that “there is no enchantment against Jacob” (Numbers 23:23). Joseph’s own testimony elsewhere is consistent: interpretations belong to God (40:8), and “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace” (41:16). The narrator records Joseph’s ruse without commending the practice it names, and the story as a whole shows that the secrets in this chapter are brought to light by God, not by a silver bowl.

wordNotes.term: נַחֵשׁ יְנַחֵשׁ (nachesh yenachesh) — indeed he divineth
wordNotes.explanation: The verb nachash is doubled for emphasis, “he surely divines.” It means to seek omens or practise divination. Laban used it of discovering by omens that God blessed him for Jacob’s sake (30:27). The law forbids it outright (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10), and it is listed among the sins of King Manasseh (2 Kings 21:6). Its use here describes the role Joseph assumes as an Egyptian lord, which the story shows to be a pretence.

wordNotes.term: הֲרֵעֹתֶם (hare‘otem) — ye have done evil
wordNotes.explanation: A form of ra‘a‘, “to do evil” or “act wickedly,” picking up the noun “evil” from verse 4. The repetition presses the moral charge. Jacob used the same verb when he complained that his sons had “dealt so ill” with him by revealing Benjamin’s existence (43:6), and it will echo in Judah’s dread of “the evil” that would come on his father (44:34).

verses.bibleText: And he overtook them, and he spake unto them these same words.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“He overtook them, and he spake unto them these same words.” The steward does exactly as he was told, word for word. The narrator does not repeat the speech, since the reader has just heard it; the brevity moves the scene quickly to the brothers’ reaction.

The pursuit recalls Laban overtaking Jacob in the hill country of Gilead to search for his stolen gods (31:23-25). That earlier scene ended with an unknown thief undiscovered. This one will end with an innocent man exposed. For the brothers, the sudden appearance of the steward on the road, after such a hospitable night, must have been bewildering. The man who had calmed them the day before now stands as their accuser.

The repetition also confirms that the accusation is scripted. The steward adds nothing of his own and subtracts nothing, so his talk of divining in verse 5 is plainly Joseph’s chosen line, delivered by a servant who knows exactly where the cup is.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּשִּׂגֵם (vayyassigem) — and he overtook them
wordNotes.explanation: From nasag, “to reach” or “overtake,” often used of a pursuer catching up with those who flee. It describes Laban reaching Jacob (31:25) and Pharaoh’s army overtaking Israel by the sea (Exodus 14:9). Here the overtaking is staged, since the brothers are not fleeing at all, but they now stand where fugitives would stand.

verses.bibleText: And they said unto him, Wherefore saith my lord these words? God forbid that thy servants should do according to this thing:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers answer with indignation: “Wherefore saith my lord these words?” They address the steward as “my lord” and call themselves “thy servants,” the deference due to the representative of a great official. Their courtesy does not soften their protest. “God forbid that thy servants should do according to this thing.” The very idea is unthinkable to them.

The protest is sincere, and on the matter of the cup it is true. Yet the reader cannot miss the irony. These are the men who once did a far worse thing than steal a goblet. Their outrage at being suspected of dishonesty shows how much they now care about their integrity, and it also sets them up to discover that integrity in one matter does not erase guilt in another. Before the day is over, Judah will admit that God has found them out (v. 16). A clear conscience about one deed can sit beside a buried wrong, and the brothers are about to learn that the God who sees does not separate the two as neatly as they do.

The same exclamation will come from Joseph’s own lips in verse 17, when he refuses to enslave all of them. Each side of the conversation declares something “far be it” from it, and each is speaking within a drama only one side understands.

wordNotes.term: חָלִילָה (chalilah) — God forbid
wordNotes.explanation: An exclamation of strong rejection, often rendered “far be it.” It is related to a root meaning “profane,” so the sense is that such a deed would be a defiling thing. The KJV supplies “God” for force; the Hebrew does not name him here. Abraham used the word when he said of the Judge of all the earth, “That be far from thee” (18:25), and David used it when he refused to harm the LORD’s anointed (1 Samuel 24:6).

verses.bibleText: Behold, the money, which we found in our sacks' mouths, we brought again unto thee out of the land of Canaan: how then should we steal out of thy lord's house silver or gold?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers support their protest with evidence. “Behold, the money, which we found in our sacks’ mouths, we brought again unto thee out of the land of Canaan.” They had done exactly that, and had confessed it to this very steward at the door of Joseph’s house (43:20-22). Men who carried silver all the way back from Canaan to return it are not likely to steal silver from their host. Their argument moves from the greater to the lesser: “how then should we steal out of thy lord’s house silver or gold?”

The argument is reasonable, and the steward knows it is true. The brothers have shown themselves honest about money. Their record on this second journey is clean, and the reader is meant to notice the improvement. On the first journey they were accused of being spies and protested, “We are true men” (42:11), while their consciences told them they were not (42:21).

The verb “steal” carries a hidden barb. Joseph had told Pharaoh’s butler that he “was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews” (40:15). The brothers ask how they could ever steal from this man’s house, unaware that they once stole the man himself. Later law would treat that kind of theft, the kidnapping and selling of a person, as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7). The money they are proud of returning is set beside the brother they never returned.

wordNotes.term: וְאֵיךְ נִגְנֹב (ve’eykh nignov) — how then should we steal
wordNotes.explanation: Ganav is the ordinary verb for stealing, used in the eighth commandment (Exodus 20:15). It also describes Rachel’s theft of Laban’s household gods (31:19) and Joseph’s own complaint that he was “stolen away” from his homeland (40:15). The question “how then” assumes that the answer is obvious: honest men who returned money would never take silver.

verses.bibleText: With whomsoever of thy servants it be found, both let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
So certain are the brothers of their innocence that they pronounce a sentence on themselves: “With whomsoever of thy servants it be found, both let him die, and we also will be my lord’s bondmen.” The guilty man would forfeit his life, and the rest would become slaves. It is a sweeping offer, made in the heat of injured honour, and it binds them more tightly than they realise.

The words echo an earlier rash oath in the family. When Laban accused Jacob of stealing his gods, Jacob replied, “With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live” (31:32), not knowing that Rachel had taken them. Now Rachel’s son will be found with the missing object, and his brothers have unknowingly set the penalty. The parallel is close enough to make a reader of Genesis hold his breath.

The brothers’ offer also reproduces Joseph’s own history. They propose that one should be counted dead while the others serve as slaves; years before, they had made Joseph a slave and let their father believe him dead. Later Israelite law did not punish theft of property with death (Exodus 22:1-4), but stealing a sacred object from a great man’s house could be regarded as sacrilege, and the brothers name the harshest penalty they can think of.

Their readiness to stand together, all accepting slavery if one is guilty, is worth noting. Whatever their motives, they speak as a united family, a change from the day when they turned against one of their own.

The offer also shows that they trust Benjamin. None of them suspects the youngest; they are as sure of him as of themselves.

wordNotes.term: וָמֵת (vamet) — let him die
wordNotes.explanation: A simple form of mut, “to die,” here expressing the penalty the brothers propose. The verb recurs through the chapter: Judah later fears that losing the lad would make his father die (vv. 22, 31). The death the brothers rashly impose on the thief is answered at the end of the chapter by Judah’s determination to spare his father from death.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Now also let it be according unto your words: he with whom it is found shall be my servant; and ye shall be blameless.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The steward seems to accept their terms, “Now also let it be according unto your words,” yet he immediately changes them. Death is dropped, and so is the enslavement of all: “he with whom it is found shall be my servant; and ye shall be blameless.” The culprit alone will be a slave, and the others will go free without guilt.

The modification sounds like fairness, and in itself it is fair. The innocent should not suffer with the guilty, and theft does not deserve death. Yet the change is the key to Joseph’s test. Had all eleven been enslaved, there would be no choice to make. By limiting the penalty to one man, the steward hands the ten their freedom and sets Benjamin apart. They can go home “blameless,” with grain for their families and an unanswerable excuse for their father. The situation now matches chapter 37: Rachel’s son in bondage in Egypt, the others free to walk away.

The steward also declines to take advantage of their rash words. People sometimes bind themselves too quickly in moments of protest, and justice does not hold them to a penalty that exceeds the offence. That restraint, even in the middle of a staged test, reflects the measured justice that later Scripture requires, where punishment answers the crime and no more (Deuteronomy 24:16; Deuteronomy 25:2-3).

wordNotes.term: נְקִיִּם (neqiyyim) — blameless
wordNotes.explanation: Naqi means clean, innocent, or free from obligation. It can describe being released from an oath (24:41; Joshua 2:17) or being innocent of guilt, as in “innocent blood” (Deuteronomy 19:10). The steward declares the other brothers free of any penalty, a status that leaves them at liberty to go home without Benjamin.

verses.bibleText: Then they speedily took down every man his sack to the ground, and opened every man his sack.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then they speedily took down every man his sack to the ground, and opened every man his sack.” The haste is the haste of men who have nothing to hide. Each brother lowers his own load and opens it at once, confident that the search will clear them and that they can be on their way.

The verb for hurrying is the same one used when Joseph “made haste” to leave the room and weep at the sight of Benjamin (43:30). Both sides of the story are moving fast, the brothers toward what they expect to be vindication, and Joseph toward a crisis he has planned and can barely endure.

The detail “every man his sack” is repeated twice in the verse. No one waits for another to go first, and no one hangs back. The scene shows a group acting together, each certain of himself and of his brothers, which makes the discovery in the next verse fall on all of them at once.

wordNotes.term: וַיְמַהֲרוּ (vaymaharu) — then they speedily
wordNotes.explanation: From mahar, “to hurry.” The verb often signals eager or urgent action, as when Abraham hastened to prepare a meal for his guests (18:6) and when Joseph hurried out to weep (43:30). Here it reveals the brothers’ confidence in their innocence.

verses.bibleText: And he searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest: and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The steward “searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest.” He follows the same order in which the brothers had been seated at the feast, to their amazement (43:33). Reuben’s sack is opened first, then the others down the line, each found free of the cup. The tension mounts with every sack. If any of them glimpsed the returned silver as the sacks were opened, the relief of being cleared would have mingled with fresh dread, but the narrator says nothing of the money and fixes attention on the cup alone.

Then comes the last sack and the terse report: “the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack.” Benjamin is named here for the first time in the chapter, at the moment he is exposed. Up to now he has been “the youngest.” Now he has a name and an accusation.

The scene is the reverse of Laban’s search. Laban went through Jacob’s tents one by one, and the stolen gods were never found because Rachel sat on them and deceived her father (31:33-35). Here Rachel’s son is innocent, the object is found, and there is no hiding place. The brothers who once concealed their crime are now confronted with a crime they did not commit.

The verb “found” threads through the chapter, used of the money (v. 8), the proposed penalty (vv. 9-10), and now the cup. It prepares for Judah’s confession that God has “found out” their iniquity (v. 16). Things hidden are being uncovered, and the brothers will soon recognise who is uncovering them (Numbers 32:23).

The order of the search also keeps the brothers watching one another. The elder sons are cleared first, and each in turn might have felt the danger pass him by. Only the youngest remains when the steward reaches into the last sack, and the one brother whose safety they had sworn to guarantee is the one exposed.

wordNotes.term: וַיְחַפֵּשׂ (vaychappes) — and he searched
wordNotes.explanation: Chippes means to search carefully, to look into hidden places. It is the verb used of Laban’s search through Jacob’s goods for his gods (31:35), linking the two scenes directly. Elsewhere God promises to “search” Jerusalem with lamps (Zephaniah 1:12), and the psalmist asks God to search out wickedness (Psalm 64:6).

verses.bibleText: Then they rent their clothes, and laded every man his ass, and returned to the city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then they rent their clothes.” The brothers respond with the ancient sign of grief and horror. In Genesis this act has a history. Reuben tore his clothes when he found the pit empty (37:29), and Jacob tore his when he saw Joseph’s bloodied coat (37:34). Genesis records no such grief among the others then; they were the ones who had brought the coat. Now all of them tear their garments for Benjamin, sharing the anguish they once inflicted on their father.

The second half of the verse is just as telling: they “laded every man his ass, and returned to the city.” The steward had told them they were free (v. 10). Only Benjamin was required. Every one of them could have gone home with his grain and let the youngest pay. No one does. They load up together and go back together, choosing to share whatever fate awaits their brother.

This is the first answer to Joseph’s test, given in action before any word is spoken. Twenty-two years earlier the brothers sat down to eat while Joseph lay in a pit (37:25). Now they will not leave Rachel’s other son alone in his trouble. The change that Joseph hoped to see begins to show here, and Judah’s words in the scenes that follow will confirm it. Their return is also a return to the man they fear most, with no idea of what he will do. They go back with nothing in their hands but their loyalty.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְרְעוּ שִׂמְלֹתָם (vayyiqre‘u simlotam) — then they rent their clothes
wordNotes.explanation: Qara‘ means to tear, and simlah is an outer garment or mantle. Tearing the garment expressed grief, dismay, or repentance. Jacob did it on learning of Joseph’s supposed death (37:34), Joshua and the elders did it after the defeat at Ai (Joshua 7:6), and Job did it when his children died (Job 1:20). The brothers now take up the gesture they once caused in their father.

verses.bibleText: And Judah and his brethren came to Joseph's house; for he was yet there: and they fell before him on the ground.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Judah and his brethren came to Joseph’s house.” For the first time the narrator names one brother ahead of the rest. Reuben, the firstborn, had made the earlier proposals (37:21-22; 42:37), but Judah persuaded Jacob to send Benjamin and pledged himself for the lad (43:3-10). Now he leads the way, and the phrase signals that the coming scene belongs to him.

Joseph “was yet there.” He has not gone about the business of the day but has stayed at home, waiting for the steward to bring them back. The brothers “fell before him on the ground.” They had bowed to him on both visits (42:6; 43:26, 28), each time unknowingly fulfilling the dreams that had once enraged them (37:7-10). This time the verb is different. They do not simply bow in courtesy; they throw themselves down, the posture of men with no defence and nothing left to offer. Egyptian reliefs show foreign petitioners prostrate before high officials in exactly this way, faces to the earth, pleading for mercy. The brothers had once mocked Joseph as “this dreamer” and plotted to see “what will become of his dreams” (37:19-20); now they lie at the feet of the dreamer without knowing who he is.

The sheaves of Joseph’s dream have bowed indeed, and more fully than he could have pictured. Yet the scene gives Joseph no satisfaction. His goal was never their humiliation but their hearts, and what they say next will show whether those hearts have changed.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְּלוּ לְפָנָיו אָרְצָה (vayyippelu lefanayv ’artsah) — and they fell before him on the ground
wordNotes.explanation: Naphal, “to fall,” here describes prostration in desperation, a stronger picture than the verb for bowing used in 37:7 and 43:26. Abigail falls before David in the same way to plead for her household (1 Samuel 25:23), and the brothers will fall before Joseph again after their father’s death, offering themselves as his servants (50:18). They have no claim left except mercy.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto them, What deed is this that ye have done? wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph speaks first and speaks harshly, as he did on their first visit (42:7). “What deed is this that ye have done?” The question recalls words heard in Genesis at moments of exposed guilt. God asked Eve, “What is this that thou hast done?” (3:13), and Pharaoh and Abimelech used similar words to Abraham (12:18; 20:9). Without knowing it, Joseph puts to his brothers the question their consciences have been asking for twenty-two years.

He adds, “wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine?” The claim repeats the steward’s line (v. 5) and keeps up the role of the all-knowing Egyptian lord. The irony is plain to the reader. Joseph’s supposed divining cup has not discovered that Benjamin is innocent; the “diviner” knows the truth only because he planted the evidence. The pretence underlines the point that the cup has no power at all. What Joseph does know about his brothers he learned by living through their cruelty, and what he will soon understand about God’s purpose he learned from God (45:5-8).

The words also push the brothers to look beyond the man in front of them. If this lord can see hidden things, then hidden things are being seen. Judah draws the right conclusion, though not the one Joseph’s words suggest: the One who sees is God (v. 16). Daniel would later tell a king that no wise man or soothsayer could reveal secrets, “But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets” (Daniel 2:27-28). Joseph’s claim, spoken as part of a disguise, ends by directing Judah’s thoughts to that God.

wordNotes.term: הֲלוֹא יְדַעְתֶּם (halo’ yeda‘tem) — wot ye not
wordNotes.explanation: “Wot” is older English for “know.” The Hebrew rhetorical question, literally “Did you not know?”, assumes the answer yes. It is the kind of question used to point out what should have been obvious, as when the prophet asks, “Have ye not known?” (Isaiah 40:21). Joseph implies that his powers were common knowledge, part of the reputation he plays upon.

wordNotes.term: אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר כָּמֹנִי (’ish ’asher kamoni) — such a man as I
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a man who is like me.” Joseph speaks of his own rank and reputation. Judah will answer in kind, “thou art even as Pharaoh” (v. 18), using a related comparison. The phrase belongs to the language of high status in Joseph’s Egyptian role, which Pharaoh had confirmed when he said there was “none so discreet and wise as thou art” (41:39).

verses.bibleText: And Judah said, What shall we say unto my lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants: behold, we are my lord's servants, both we, and he also with whom the cup is found.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah answers with three questions that admit he has no defence: “What shall we say unto my lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear ourselves?” The evidence is overwhelming; the cup lay in Benjamin’s sack, and nothing the brothers can say will remove it. Judah does not accuse the steward of planting it, though the returned money must have suggested as much. He does not blame Benjamin. He gives up any attempt at self-justification.

Then comes the sentence that makes this chapter a turning point in Genesis: “God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants.” Judah has just protested their innocence of theft (v. 8), so he cannot mean that they stole the cup. He is speaking of an older guilt, the sin against Joseph that had haunted them since the day they heard his cries from the pit. On the first visit they had said to one another, “We are verily guilty concerning our brother” (42:21). Now Judah says it, in effect, in the presence of an Egyptian lord, to whom the words must have sounded like a confession of the theft. Only Joseph, and the reader, understand what he means.

Judah sees God’s hand behind the strange events. The returned money, the seating by age, the cup in Benjamin’s sack, all point to One who has been tracking them. Moses would later warn Israel, “be sure your sin will find you out” (Numbers 32:23). Judah has learned that it does. Concealed sin is never hidden from God; it is only waiting to be uncovered, and the uncovering is itself a mercy, since sin acknowledged can be forgiven. David found this when he stopped keeping silence and confessed, and the LORD forgave the iniquity of his sin (Psalm 32:3-5). the one who confesses and forsakes sin “shall have mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

Judah’s offer follows from his confession: “behold, we are my lord’s servants, both we, and he also with whom the cup is found.” He drops the rash death penalty of verse 9 but refuses to separate Benjamin from the rest. If one is to be a slave, all will be. The brothers who once sold a brother into slavery in Egypt now offer to share slavery in Egypt with his brother. Their solidarity with Rachel’s son is the clearest sign yet that God’s work in them has gone deep.

wordNotes.term: הָאֱלֹהִים מָצָא אֶת־עֲוֹן עֲבָדֶיךָ (ha’elohim matsa’ ’et-‘avon ‘avadeykha) — God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Avon is iniquity or guilt, often including the burden of consequence that sin brings (4:13, where Cain says his “punishment” is greater than he can bear). Matsa’, “to find,” is the chapter’s recurring verb: the money was found (v. 8), the cup was found (v. 12), and now God has found their guilt. The cup is the occasion; the real discovery is their sin against Joseph, which Judah acknowledges before God.

wordNotes.term: וּמַה־נִּצְטַדָּק (umah-nitstaddaq) — how shall we clear ourselves
wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form of tsadaq, “to be righteous” or “in the right,” meaning to justify oneself or prove oneself innocent. This is the only place the reflexive form occurs in the Old Testament. Judah gives up self-justification, the same attitude Job reached when he asked how a man could be just with God (Job 9:2) and that Paul describes when every mouth is stopped before God (Romans 3:19).

verses.bibleText: And he said, God forbid that I should do so: but the man in whose hand the cup is found, he shall be my servant; and as for you, get you up in peace unto your father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph refuses Judah’s offer in the same words the brothers had used on the road: “God forbid that I should do so.” He insists on the steward’s terms. “The man in whose hand the cup is found, he shall be my servant; and as for you, get you up in peace unto your father.” Only Benjamin will stay.

The ruling sounds just. The innocent should not be punished for the guilty, and Joseph presents himself as a fair judge who will not enslave ten men for one man’s crime. Yet the fairness is the final turn of the test. Judah has offered solidarity; Joseph now makes solidarity costly by removing any need for it. The ten are free. Their father is waiting for grain. No one could blame them for going home. Joseph has re-created the choice of Dothan exactly: Rachel’s son in bondage and the others released to return to Jacob with a story to tell.

The parting words carry a sharp irony: “get you up in peace unto your father.” Shalom is the word Joseph had used when he asked whether their father was well (43:27). There can be no peace for Jacob if they return without Benjamin, and everyone in the room knows it, Joseph included. Jacob had said that losing Benjamin would bring his gray hairs “with sorrow to the grave” (42:38). The peace Joseph offers is the very thing that would destroy their father.

Judah’s reply, which fills the rest of the chapter, is triggered by this phrase. He will explain, at length and with great feeling, why going up to his father without the lad is impossible. The test has reached the point where words reveal the heart.

wordNotes.term: עֲלוּ לְשָׁלוֹם (‘alu leshalom) — get you up in peace
wordNotes.explanation: Shalom means wholeness and well-being, not merely the absence of conflict. It was used of Jacob’s welfare in 43:27-28 and of the peace Jacob hoped to return in at Bethel (28:21). “Go up” is the regular expression for travelling from Egypt to the higher land of Canaan (45:9). Joseph’s blessing is formally correct but empty in this situation, which is what moves Judah to speak.

verses.bibleText: Then Judah came near unto him, and said, Oh my lord, let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word in my lord's ears, and let not thine anger burn against thy servant: for thou art even as Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Judah came near unto him.” Joseph has pronounced sentence and dismissed the others. Protocol would have the brothers withdraw. Instead Judah steps forward, uninvited, toward the most powerful man in Egypt after the king. The approach itself is a risk, and his opening words acknowledge it: “Oh my lord, let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word in my lord’s ears, and let not thine anger burn against thy servant: for thou art even as Pharaoh.”

Every phrase is courteous. Judah calls himself “thy servant” and Joseph “my lord” repeatedly. He asks permission to speak and begs that his boldness not provoke anger. He acknowledges that Joseph holds the authority of Pharaoh himself, as Pharaoh had declared (41:40-44), with power to condemn or to pardon and no one above him in the matter. That recognition is also an appeal: a man with such power is free to show mercy.

What follows is the longest speech in Genesis, seventeen verses of reasoned, passionate pleading. Judah does not argue Benjamin’s innocence, which would be useless after the evidence of the cup. He does not bargain or threaten. He tells the story of his father’s love and grief, and he lets that story make the case. Its key word is “father,” which recurs again and again, from the first question Joseph asked (v. 19) to Judah’s final cry (v. 34).

The man who once said “Come, and let us sell him” (37:27) now draws near to plead for the son of Rachel. Judah stands as an intercessor, placing himself between the judge and the condemned. In that role he anticipates the One who would come from his tribe and who “ever liveth to make intercession” for those who come to God by him (Hebrews 7:25).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגַּשׁ (vayyiggash) — then Judah came near
wordNotes.explanation: Nagash means to draw near or approach, frequently in contexts of petition, confrontation, or worship. Abraham “drew near” to plead for Sodom (18:23), Jacob came near to his blind father to receive the blessing (27:22), and priests “come near” to minister before the LORD (Exodus 28:43). Judah approaches as one who has something urgent to ask of a superior.

wordNotes.term: כִּי כָמוֹךָ כְּפַרְעֹה (ki khamokha kefar‘oh) — for thou art even as Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “for like you is like Pharaoh,” a doubled comparison meaning “you are the equal of Pharaoh.” The king of Egypt was regarded as divine, so comparison with him was the highest honour a subject could receive. Judah’s words recognise the authority Pharaoh had given Joseph over all the land (41:44).

verses.bibleText: My lord asked his servants, saying, Have ye a father, or a brother?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah begins at the beginning: “My lord asked his servants, saying, Have ye a father, or a brother?” He frames the whole affair as starting from Joseph’s own question. In the account of the first visit, the brothers volunteered their family details while defending themselves against the charge of spying (42:11-13). Later, however, they told Jacob that the man “asked us straitly of our state, and of our kindred” (43:7). Judah’s summary agrees with that report and leaves out the accusation of spying and Simeon’s imprisonment altogether.

The tactful selection serves his purpose. Benjamin is in Egypt because the lord of Egypt asked about him and insisted on seeing him. Judah gently places the responsibility for the lad’s presence on Joseph, without a word of complaint. And by opening with the words “father” and “brother,” he announces the two subjects that will carry his whole appeal.

The question itself is ordinary, the kind any official might ask of foreigners. Yet for Joseph it was never ordinary. Behind his inquiry lay the longing to know whether his father and his full brother were still alive, and Judah’s retelling now brings that longing back before him.

wordNotes.term: הֲיֵשׁ־לָכֶם אָב אוֹ־אָח (hayesh-lakhem ’av ’o-’ach) — have ye a father, or a brother?
wordNotes.explanation: A simple question, literally “Is there to you a father or a brother?” Joseph had asked after their father’s welfare at the feast (43:27), and the brothers later reported that he had pressed them on their kindred (43:7). By quoting it, Judah fixes the two relationships that drive the rest of his speech.

verses.bibleText: And we said unto my lord, We have a father, an old man, and a child of his old age, a little one; and his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loveth him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah recalls their answer: “We have a father, an old man, and a child of his old age, a little one; and his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loveth him.” Each phrase adds weight. The father is old. Benjamin is the “child of his old age,” the very description once given to Joseph (37:3). He is “a little one,” a term of affection rather than literal age, since Benjamin was a grown man who would soon be listed with sons of his own (46:21). To the old man, he is still the youngest and most protected.

Then Judah says, “his brother is dead.” He speaks these words to that brother’s face. The brothers had told the lie of Joseph’s death to their father years ago, and they seem to have come to believe it themselves; no one had heard of Joseph since. Joseph listens to his own death reported by the man who proposed selling him. He alone in the room knows that the dead brother is alive and that the one weeping inwardly is the man on the throne.

Most striking is the last clause: “his father loveth him.” Judah states the favouritism plainly. Jacob loves Benjamin as he once loved Joseph more than all his children, and that love once filled the brothers with such hatred that “they could not speak peaceably unto him” (37:4). Now Judah names the same partiality without a trace of bitterness and makes it the ground of his plea. Jacob has not changed. His sons have. They have come to accept that their father’s heart is bound to Rachel’s children, and instead of resenting it they want to protect it.

wordNotes.term: יֶלֶד זְקֻנִים קָטָן (yeled zequnim qatan) — a child of his old age, a little one
wordNotes.explanation: Zequnim, “old age,” is the same word used when Joseph is called “the son of his old age” (37:3), and Isaac was born to Abraham in his old age (21:2, 7). Yeled, “child,” and qatan, “little” or “youngest,” express affection and family rank more than literal years. Judah presents Benjamin as Jacob sees him.

verses.bibleText: And thou saidst unto thy servants, Bring him down unto me, that I may set mine eyes upon him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And thou saidst unto thy servants, Bring him down unto me, that I may set mine eyes upon him.” Judah recalls Joseph’s demand in terms that suggest kindly interest. The account in chapter 42 records Joseph’s requirement more sternly, as a test of their honesty (42:15, 20, 34). Judah presents it in its most favourable light: the lord of Egypt wanted to see the boy.

The phrase “set mine eyes upon him” is the Hebrew idiom for looking upon someone with favour and care. Judah does not say so openly, but his wording implies a question. The great man asked to see Benjamin in order to look on him kindly. Can it be that he brought him all this way only to enslave him? Judah holds Joseph to the meaning of his own words, respectfully, without a hint of accusation.

There is a further irony in the phrase. Joseph had indeed wanted to see Benjamin, more than Judah could guess, and when he did, his heart was so stirred that he left the room to weep (43:29-30). Judah appeals to a kindness that is more real than he knows.

wordNotes.term: וְאָשִׂימָה עֵינִי עָלָיו (ve’asimah ‘eyni ‘alayv) — that I may set mine eyes upon him
wordNotes.explanation: “To set the eye upon” someone usually means to look on him with favour and attention. God promises the exiles, “I will set mine eyes upon them for good” (Jeremiah 24:6), and Nebuchadnezzar orders that Jeremiah be looked after: “look well to him” (Jeremiah 39:12). Judah implies that Joseph’s request expressed good intentions toward Benjamin.

verses.bibleText: And we said unto my lord, The lad cannot leave his father: for if he should leave his father, his father would die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And we said unto my lord, The lad cannot leave his father: for if he should leave his father, his father would die.” This reply does not appear in the account of the first visit. It may have been said and not recorded, or Judah may be summarising the brothers’ reluctance in its strongest form. Either way, it adds something new: the brothers say they warned the ruler from the start that separating Benjamin from Jacob could be fatal.

The repetition of “his father” within one sentence is deliberate. Judah keeps the old man before Joseph’s eyes. The concern is not first for Benjamin’s comfort but for Jacob’s life. The brothers had once been willing to break their father’s heart; now their argument is built entirely on protecting it.

The phrase “his father would die” prepares for the heart of the appeal in verses 30-31. Judah is laying the groundwork step by step, so that when he finally asks for mercy, the cost of refusing it is already clear.

wordNotes.term: הַנַּעַר (hanna‘ar) — the lad
wordNotes.explanation: Na‘ar can describe anyone from an infant to a young man; it often marks a person as young or dependent rather than giving an exact age. Joseph was called a na‘ar at seventeen (37:2), and Ishmael as a boy was “the lad” whom God heard (21:17). Judah uses the word repeatedly in this speech, presenting Benjamin as the youth for whom he is responsible.

verses.bibleText: And thou saidst unto thy servants, Except your youngest brother come down with you, ye shall see my face no more.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And thou saidst unto thy servants, Except your youngest brother come down with you, ye shall see my face no more.” This is the condition Joseph had laid down (42:15, 20), and it became the decisive argument in Jacob’s household. Judah had quoted it to his father twice, almost word for word (43:3, 5).

To be denied a ruler’s face was to be shut out from his presence and favour. Absalom lived two years in Jerusalem without seeing King David’s face, an exile within the city (2 Samuel 14:24). For the brothers, not seeing the face of the man who controlled Egypt’s grain meant starvation. Judah’s point is that they had no choice. Benjamin came because Joseph required it, and the brothers obeyed.

Judah repeats the condition without resentment. He does not call it unreasonable or complain of the hardship it caused. He simply sets it beside the father’s grief that follows, so that Joseph can see the two forces that held the family in a vise: the ruler’s demand on one side and Jacob’s fear on the other.

wordNotes.term: לֹא תֹסִפוּן לִרְאוֹת פָּנָי (lo’ tosifun lir’ot panay) — ye shall see my face no more
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “you shall not add to see my face.” Seeing someone’s face means access to him. Jacob had said of Esau that seeing his face was like seeing the face of God (33:10), and Moses told Pharaoh he would see his face no more (Exodus 10:29). Joseph had made access to himself, and so to grain, depend on Benjamin’s coming.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass when we came up unto thy servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass when we came up unto thy servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.” Judah summarises the brothers’ report to Jacob after the first journey (42:29-34). They had passed on the governor’s demand faithfully. The report was honest, and the brothers kept nothing back from their father this time, a contrast with the long silence they had kept about Joseph.

The phrase “thy servant my father” stands out. Judah calls Jacob Joseph’s servant, the polite form of speech toward a superior, as the brothers had already done at the feast (43:28). Yet the words fulfil more than etiquette. Joseph’s second dream showed the sun and moon bowing to him, and Jacob had rebuked him for it (37:10). Now the patriarch is spoken of, in Joseph’s hearing, as his servant.

Judah moves quickly through this step. The speech is not a full history but a selection, and he hurries toward the words of his father, which he will quote at length in the verses that follow.

wordNotes.term: עַבְדְּךָ אָבִי (‘avdekha ’avi) — thy servant my father
wordNotes.explanation: A courteous expression in which a speaker refers to himself or his family as the servant of the one he addresses. The brothers used it of Jacob before Joseph at the feast (43:28), and the same courtesy appears in Jacob’s messages to Esau (32:4, 18). In this setting it also echoes Joseph’s dream of his father bowing to him (37:10).

verses.bibleText: And our father said, Go again, and buy us a little food.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And our father said, Go again, and buy us a little food.” Judah moves to the second journey. The grain from the first trip had run out (43:2), and the famine left Jacob no alternative. His words are modest: “a little food,” only enough to survive. The family was not seeking plenty but bare life.

By quoting his father directly, Judah lets Joseph hear Jacob’s voice for the first time in more than twenty years. Every quotation in the speech brings the old man closer to the room. Joseph learns from these words that his father is still providing for the household, still sending his sons out, and still hungry. The request also explains why the brothers were in Egypt at all: they had come because their father sent them in need, and they had brought Benjamin because they could not come without him.

The pressure of famine forms the background of the whole story. Jacob had once said, “that we may live, and not die” (42:2), and Judah had used the same words in persuading him to let Benjamin go (43:8). The need for bread pushed the family down to Egypt, toward the brother they had lost.

wordNotes.term: מְעַט־אֹכֶל (me‘at-’okhel) — a little food
wordNotes.explanation: Me‘at means “a little” or “a few,” and ’okhel is food in general. Jacob’s request is restrained, asking only for enough to live. The same phrase appears in his original instruction (43:2). The word me‘at was also used of the small gift of balm and honey Jacob sent to the ruler (43:11).

verses.bibleText: And we said, We cannot go down: if our youngest brother be with us, then will we go down: for we may not see the man's face, except our youngest brother be with us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And we said, We cannot go down: if our youngest brother be with us, then will we go down: for we may not see the man’s face, except our youngest brother be with us.” Judah summarises the argument he himself had made to Jacob (43:3-5). The brothers refused to go without Benjamin, not out of stubbornness but because the governor’s condition left them no choice.

Judah repeats “youngest brother” twice in one sentence and ties the journey entirely to Benjamin’s presence. He is establishing that the brothers acted in good faith at every step: Joseph demanded Benjamin, the brothers told their father, and they insisted on obeying Joseph’s word even against their father’s wishes. If Benjamin is now in danger, it is because they did exactly what the lord of Egypt required. The speech is building a case in which mercy seems the only fitting response.

The verse also hints at the struggle that went on in Jacob’s house. The brothers’ refusal stood against their father’s will, and Jacob had resisted until the food ran out (43:1-2). Judah does not dwell on that conflict, but Joseph can hear in the summary that the decision to bring Benjamin was made under heavy pressure and with great reluctance. It was Judah who finally broke the deadlock by offering himself as surety (43:8-9), a fact he will reveal in verse 32.

wordNotes.term: לֹא נוּכַל לָרֶדֶת (lo’ nukhal laredet) — we cannot go down
wordNotes.explanation: Yakhol, “to be able,” with a negative expresses impossibility. Going “down” to Egypt is the regular expression for travel from the hill country of Canaan (42:2-3). The brothers had told their father the journey was impossible without Benjamin, just as Judah will say it is impossible for him to go up without him (v. 34).

verses.bibleText: And thy servant my father said unto us, Ye know that my wife bare me two sons:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Judah quotes his father’s own words: “Ye know that my wife bare me two sons.” This sentence is new to the reader; the narrative of chapters 42 and 43 does not record it. It reveals how Jacob spoke to his sons, and it is painful to hear. Jacob had four wives who bore him twelve sons, yet to him there was only one “wife,” Rachel, and only two sons who truly counted, Joseph and Benjamin.

Judah’s mother was Leah, the wife Jacob never wanted (29:30-31). Judah himself was one of the sons Jacob’s words passed over. Yet he repeats the sentence before an Egyptian lord without protest, apology, or edge. He does not soften it or correct it. He accepts it as the truth of his father’s heart and uses it to show how much Benjamin means to the old man. The resentment that once drove the brothers to hate Joseph for his father’s love has given way to compassion for a father who has suffered.

The statement is consistent with the way Genesis speaks of Rachel elsewhere. In the list of Jacob’s family going down to Egypt, Rachel alone is called “Jacob’s wife” (46:19). Jacob’s love for her had been the story of his life since the well at Haran (29:18, 20), and her early death on the road to Bethlehem left him clinging to her two sons (35:19).

For Joseph, hearing these words must have been overwhelming. His father still remembers his mother as “my wife,” still counts him as one of only two sons, and still grieves. And the brother who once sold him repeats it all with sympathy, not envy.

wordNotes.term: אִשְׁתִּי (’ishti) — my wife
wordNotes.explanation: ’Ishshah means woman or wife. Jacob had earlier spoken of “my wives” (30:26; 31:50), but here he uses the singular of Rachel alone, and the narrator later calls Rachel “Jacob’s wife” in a list where the others are named as mothers only (46:19). The usage shows how fully Rachel held Jacob’s affection, a fact Judah now accepts without bitterness.

verses.bibleText: And the one went out from me, and I said, Surely he is torn in pieces; and I saw him not since:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Judah continues quoting Jacob: “And the one went out from me, and I said, Surely he is torn in pieces; and I saw him not since.” These are the words Jacob spoke when he saw the blood-stained coat, “Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces” (37:33). Judah repeats them to Joseph, who hears for the first time how his father explained his disappearance and how he still speaks of it.

The phrase “went out from me” recalls the day Jacob sent Joseph from the vale of Hebron to see how his brothers fared (37:13-14). Jacob blames himself, perhaps, for sending the boy; he certainly remembers that it was from his own presence that Joseph went. “I saw him not since” has a hint of unresolved doubt. A man who believed absolutely that his son was dead might not add that he had never seen him again. Jacob may have half suspected that the truth was other than his sons had told him (42:36).

For Judah the quotation is costly. He was the one who proposed the sale (37:26-27), and the brothers together had sent the coat that led to Jacob’s conclusion. In repeating his father’s words, Judah is quoting the result of his own deception. He does not confess it here to the Egyptian lord; he has already confessed before God (v. 16). But the words lie between him and Joseph, and both of them know what they mean.

wordNotes.term: טָרֹף טֹרָף (tarof toraf) — surely he is torn in pieces
wordNotes.explanation: The verb taraf, “to tear” or “rend,” used of wild beasts attacking prey, is doubled for emphasis. It is the exact phrase Jacob used over Joseph’s coat (37:33). The law later relieved a shepherd of responsibility for an animal “torn of beasts” if he brought evidence (Exodus 22:13), the kind of evidence the brothers had falsely supplied with the coat.

verses.bibleText: And if ye take this also from me, and mischief befall him, ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob’s words conclude: “And if ye take this also from me, and mischief befall him, ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.” The patriarch had said nearly the same thing when he first refused to let Benjamin go (42:38). “Take this also from me” holds the sons responsible. Jacob had already accused them of bereaving him of Joseph and Simeon (42:36), and he warns them that losing Benjamin would finish him.

The word “mischief” translates a term for disaster or fatal harm. Jacob had used it twice before, fearing that some accident would befall Benjamin on the road (42:4, 38). Now, in Judah’s retelling, the feared disaster has come, not by the dangers of travel but by the cup in the lad’s sack.

“Ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave” pictures the old man going down to death in misery instead of peace. The word for “grave” is she’ol, the common Old Testament term for the place of the dead. Jacob first spoke of going down to she’ol mourning for Joseph (37:35). He does not picture an afterlife of conscious activity, nor a reunion with Joseph in some spirit world. He pictures death itself, the end of life, and the grief that would accompany his last days. Scripture consistently presents she’ol as the realm of silence where “there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom” (Ecclesiastes 9:10), and where the dead do not praise God (Psalm 6:5). The dead rest there until the resurrection; the hope of the faithful lies in the God who “bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up” (1 Samuel 2:6), and Jesus spoke of the day when all that are in the graves shall hear his voice (John 5:28-29).

Jacob’s fear will not be realised. When the brothers return, it will be with the news that Joseph is alive, and the old man will say, “I will go and see him before I die” (45:28). God has a better ending than the one Jacob dreads.

wordNotes.term: שְׁאֹלָה (she’olah) — to the grave
wordNotes.explanation: She’ol, here with a suffix meaning “toward,” is the Old Testament name for the realm of the dead, the grave viewed as the common destination of all who die. It is described as a place of silence and darkness without knowledge or activity (Ecclesiastes 9:10; Psalm 6:5). Jacob speaks of going down there in grief (37:35), meaning death itself, not a conscious existence apart from the body. The righteous hope for redemption from its power (Psalm 49:15).

wordNotes.term: אָסוֹן (’ason) — mischief
wordNotes.explanation: ’Ason means fatal harm or disaster. Outside Genesis it occurs only in the law concerning injury to a pregnant woman (Exodus 21:22-23). In Genesis it appears only in Jacob’s fears for Benjamin (42:4, 38), which Judah repeats here. Jacob’s worst fear for his youngest son is expressed in this one word.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore when I come to thy servant my father, and the lad be not with us; seeing that his life is bound up in the lad's life;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now therefore” marks the turn from narrative to appeal. Judah has finished recounting the past; he now draws its consequence for the present. “When I come to thy servant my father, and the lad be not with us; seeing that his life is bound up in the lad’s life.” He pictures the moment of arrival in Canaan, the old man looking past the returning sons for the one face that matters to him, and not finding it.

The phrase “his life is bound up in the lad’s life” is one of the most moving in the speech. Jacob’s very existence is tied to Benjamin. Losing him would not be one more sorrow among many; it would cut the cord that holds the old man to life. Judah is not exaggerating for effect. He has watched his father’s grief for twenty-two years, and he knows what another loss would do.

This insight into his father’s heart is new in Judah. When the brothers brought the coat to Jacob, they saw his anguish and his refusal to be comforted (37:34-35), yet they kept silent for two decades. Something has changed. Judah has known grief of his own, losing two sons and his wife (38:7-12), and that sorrow may have opened his eyes to his father’s. Whatever the means, God has given him a heart that feels another’s pain.

The Hebrew word used twice here is nephesh, often translated “soul.” Here it plainly means life, the living self, the whole person. Jacob’s life and Benjamin’s life are so joined that the death of one would mean the death of the other.

wordNotes.term: וְנַפְשׁוֹ קְשׁוּרָה בְנַפְשׁוֹ (venafsho qeshurah venafsho) — his life is bound up in the lad’s life
wordNotes.explanation: Nephesh is the living being, the person as a whole or the life that animates him (2:7). Qashar means to tie or bind, as the midwife tied a scarlet thread on Zerah’s hand (38:28). The same image describes Jonathan’s love for David: “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” (1 Samuel 18:1). Jacob’s life is so bound to Benjamin’s that losing the son would end the father. The phrase speaks of the whole person’s life, not of a separable soul.

verses.bibleText: It shall come to pass, when he seeth that the lad is not with us, that he will die: and thy servants shall bring down the gray hairs of thy servant our father with sorrow to the grave.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“It shall come to pass, when he seeth that the lad is not with us, that he will die.” Judah states the consequence without softening it. He then repeats his father’s own words, but with a change of subject: “thy servants shall bring down the gray hairs of thy servant our father with sorrow to the grave.” In verse 29 Jacob said “ye shall bring down”; now Judah says it of the brothers themselves. He accepts the responsibility.

The Hebrew word for “sorrow” here differs from that in verse 29. There Jacob spoke of going down to the grave “in evil,” in misery or calamity; here Judah speaks of “grief,” the inward anguish of a broken heart. Both describe what the brothers once caused and what they now refuse to cause again.

The contrast with chapter 37 is sharp. Then the brothers deliberately let their father believe his son was dead and watched his grief without a word. Now Judah cannot bear the thought of bringing the same sorrow on him again. He who once gave no thought to his father’s suffering now pleads to prevent it.

Judah’s willingness to say “thy servants shall bring down” marks a moral shift. He no longer speaks as though events simply happen to the family. He names the brothers as the ones who would cause their father’s death, and so he takes ownership of the outcome before it happens.

wordNotes.term: בְּיָגוֹן (beyagon) — with sorrow
wordNotes.explanation: Yagon means grief or anguish, the inner pain of sorrow. It is the word Jacob used when he first refused to let Benjamin go (42:38). The psalmist laments that his life is spent “with grief” (Psalm 31:10), and Jeremiah asks why he was born to see “labour and sorrow” (Jeremiah 20:18). Judah now uses it of the grief the brothers would inflict.

verses.bibleText: For thy servant became surety for the lad unto my father, saying, If I bring him not unto thee, then I shall bear the blame to my father for ever.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For thy servant became surety for the lad unto my father, saying, If I bring him not unto thee, then I shall bear the blame to my father for ever.” Judah now reveals what Joseph did not know: he had personally pledged himself for Benjamin’s safety. The narrative recorded this pledge (43:9), but Joseph had no way of knowing it until now.

The pledge explains why Judah, rather than Reuben or any other brother, steps forward. Reuben had offered his two sons as security (42:37), a rash offer Jacob refused. Judah offered himself. He took on Benjamin’s fate as his own. If the lad did not return, Judah would “bear the blame for ever.” He had placed his whole life under obligation for his brother.

This is the language of suretyship. A surety was one who guaranteed another’s debt or obligation, standing in his place if he failed. Proverbs warns against becoming surety lightly for strangers (Proverbs 6:1-2; 11:15), because the surety becomes liable for what he did not owe. Judah had done exactly that for his brother, and now the bill has come due.

The New Testament takes up this language for Christ. “By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament” (Hebrews 7:22). Christ guarantees the covenant by pledging himself, standing liable for those he represents. Judah’s pledge for Benjamin, made in Canaan and honoured in Egypt at the cost of his freedom, gives a human picture of what it means for one person to answer with his own life for another.

The pledge also shows that Judah’s change was not born in this crisis. It had already shown itself in Canaan, when he set his own life against the risk of the journey. What Joseph now hears is the fruit of a decision made before the cup was ever hidden.

wordNotes.term: עָרַב (‘arav) — became surety
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Arav means to pledge oneself, to stand as guarantor for another. Judah used it when he told his father, “I will be surety for him” (43:9). Proverbs repeatedly warns about striking hands as surety (Proverbs 6:1; 17:18), and the psalmist asks God to be surety for him (Psalm 119:122). Hebrews calls Christ the surety, Greek engyos, of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22).

wordNotes.term: וְחָטָאתִי לְאָבִי כָּל־הַיָּמִים (vechata’ti le’avi kol-hayyamim) — then I shall bear the blame to my father for ever
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “I shall have sinned against my father all the days.” Chata’ is the regular verb for sin. Judah accepts that failing to bring Benjamin back would make him guilty before his father for life. It is the same verb Joseph used in refusing to “sin against God” (39:9) and Reuben in recalling his plea, “Do not sin against the child” (42:22).

verses.bibleText: Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren.” This is the climax of Judah’s speech and one of the high points of Genesis. He does not ask that all be released or that the penalty be cancelled. He asks to take Benjamin’s place. Let Judah remain as a slave in Egypt; let the lad go home.

The offer reverses everything Judah once did. Twenty-two years earlier he had said, “Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites” (37:27), and Joseph was carried into slavery in Egypt. Now Judah offers himself into slavery in Egypt so that Rachel’s other son can go free. The man who sold a brother for silver now gives himself for a brother. He offers it for the sake of a father who loved Benjamin more than him, and of a brother who was favoured over him. Judah has become an entirely different man.

The word “instead of” is the same one used when Abraham offered the ram “in the stead of his son” on Mount Moriah (22:13). There God provided a substitute for Isaac. Here Judah offers himself as a substitute for Benjamin. This is the first time in Scripture that one person voluntarily offers to bear another’s penalty in his place, and it points forward to a greater substitution.

Judah’s descendant, the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), would come to serve and, beyond serving, to give his life. Christ “took upon him the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and “the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Judah offered himself for an innocent brother; Christ offered himself for the guilty, “the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). “The LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). Judah’s substitution saved one brother from slavery; Christ’s saves all who believe from sin and death.

The comparison has limits. Judah himself was a sinner who needed forgiveness, and his offer could not atone for anyone. Yet God was shaping the tribe from which the Saviour would come, and in this moment Judah shows the self-giving love that would be perfectly fulfilled in his greater Son.

wordNotes.term: יֵשֶׁב־נָא עַבְדְּךָ תַּחַת הַנַּעַר (yeshev-na’ ‘avdekha tachat hanna‘ar) — let thy servant abide instead of the lad
wordNotes.explanation: Tachat means “under,” “in place of,” or “instead of.” It is the word used of the ram offered “in the stead of” Isaac (22:13) and of evil returned “for” good (44:4). Judah asks to remain as a slave in Benjamin’s place, the first voluntary human substitution in Scripture. The idea of one standing in another’s place reaches its fulfilment in Christ, who died for sinners (2 Corinthians 5:21).

verses.bibleText: For how shall I go up to my father, and the lad be not with me? lest peradventure I see the evil that shall come on my father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For how shall I go up to my father, and the lad be not with me? lest peradventure I see the evil that shall come on my father.” Judah ends where he began, with his father. He cannot face the old man without Benjamin. He would rather spend his life as a slave in Egypt than watch his father die of grief.

The word “evil” has run through the chapter. The steward accused the brothers of returning evil for good (v. 4) and of doing evil in taking the cup (v. 5). Now Judah speaks of the evil that would “find” his father, using the same verb that has tracked the money, the cup, and the brothers’ guilt. Once the brothers brought evil on their father without a second thought. Now Judah would give up his freedom rather than see it fall on him again.

The contrast with chapter 37 could not be clearer. Then Judah and his brothers watched their father weep over a blood-stained coat and did nothing. Now Judah says he cannot bear even to see the evil that would come on him. The man who once caused his father’s grief now begs to prevent it.

Judah’s speech is over, and it has done its work. Joseph’s test was meant to reveal whether his brothers had changed, and Judah’s plea has answered beyond doubt. They will not abandon Rachel’s son. They care for their father. And one of them is willing to give up everything for his brother. Joseph cannot hold back any longer. The next verse will find him sending everyone from the room and weeping aloud as he makes himself known (45:1-2). Love that lays down its life for another, of which Jesus said there is no greater (John 15:13), has broken through.

Notice too that Judah never asks for his own freedom. Every argument in the speech is for someone else: for Benjamin to go home, for his father to live. The whole appeal is spent on others.

wordNotes.term: בָרָע אֲשֶׁר יִמְצָא אֶת־אָבִי (vara‘ ’asher yimtsa’ ’et-’avi) — the evil that shall come on my father
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the evil that will find my father.” Ra‘ is evil, harm, or calamity, and matsa’, “to find,” is the chapter’s recurring verb. The phrase gathers both threads: the evil charged against the brothers (vv. 4-5) and the finding that has driven the chapter (vv. 12, 16). Judah fears that calamity will find his father as God has found out their sin. Moses used the same verb when warning that troubles would “come upon” Israel (Deuteronomy 31:17).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How can anyone tell whether a person who once did great wrong has truly changed?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Joseph’s test placed his brothers where they had stood twenty-two years before, and their response showed that God had changed them: they owned their guilt before God, refused to abandon Rachel’s son, and Judah offered himself as a slave in his brother’s place, a pattern that points to Christ, the Son of Judah who gave himself for others.
discussionQuestions: How does Joseph’s plan re-create the situation of chapter 37, and what choice does it set before the brothers?
Why does Judah say “God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants” when they had not stolen the cup?
What does Judah’s speech add to what we already knew about Jacob, the brothers, and the earlier journeys?
How has Judah changed since he proposed selling Joseph, and what events in chapters 38 and 43 help explain the change?
In what ways does Judah’s offer to stay instead of Benjamin foreshadow Christ, and where does the comparison fall short?
commonMisunderstandings: Joseph’s talk of divining by the cup is part of his disguise as an Egyptian official; Scripture forbids divination (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10), and Joseph credits God alone with revealing secrets (41:16).
Joseph’s test was not revenge; its aim was to learn whether his brothers’ hearts had changed so that the family could be reconciled.
Judah’s confession in verse 16 is not an admission of theft; he sees God’s hand bringing their old sin against Joseph to light.
Judah’s offer does not atone for anyone; it points ahead to Christ, whose substitution is fuller, for he died for the guilty and was himself without sin.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the test and the change together. God used the pressure Joseph applied to bring old sin into the open, and the brothers met it with confession and self-giving love. Let Judah’s plea, with its concern for his father and its offer to stand in Benjamin’s place, carry the weight of the lesson.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: God still brings hidden sin to light so that he can heal it. Confess what he has found out, and trust the greater Son of Judah, who took the place of the guilty and bore their penalty, to make you a person who gives yourself for others.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Confession and substitution: God brings sin to light so that sinners will acknowledge it, and he provides a Substitute, foreshadowed in Judah and fulfilled in Christ, who takes the place of the guilty.
flow: Joseph’s brothers had hidden their sin against him for twenty-two years, yet it troubled their consciences.
When Benjamin was accused, Judah confessed, “God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants”: no one can hide sin from God.
Judah, once the man who sold his brother, offered to remain a slave instead of Benjamin so that the lad could go home to his father.
Christ, born of the tribe of Judah, went further, giving his life in the place of sinners who deserved death.
Confess your sin to God and accept the Substitute he has provided.
simpleIllustrations: A man co-signs a loan for a friend; when the friend cannot pay, the debt becomes his. Judah had co-signed for Benjamin with his own life.
An old wound can be covered for years, yet it will not heal until it is opened and cleaned; God opened the brothers’ guilt so that it could be healed.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you acknowledge the sin God has found out in your life and receive Christ, who took your place?
cautions: Do not present Joseph’s pretence of divination as approval of fortune-telling or occult practices; Scripture condemns them.
Do not suggest that Judah earned forgiveness by his offer; his change was the fruit of God’s work in him.
Handle the theme of family favouritism with care, since many listeners carry wounds from it.

reflectionQuestions: Is there an old sin I have hidden that God is bringing back to my conscience so that I will confess it?
When I am given an easy way out at someone else’s expense, which way do I choose?
Can I speak about someone who is loved more than I am without resentment, as Judah did?
Whose burden am I willing to carry, even at cost to myself?
How does Christ’s willingness to take my place change the way I treat others?
